The Circular Innovation Incubation Program kicked off with a two-day Entry Bootcamp on 13 and 14 October 2026 at NSRCEL, bringing together 12 startups building solutions in Plastic Circularity, Glass Circularity and Climate-Smart Agriculture. 

The Circular Innovation Incubation Program is an initiative by Pernod Ricard India Foundation in partnership with NSRCEL. 

The bootcamp brought together founders, industry leaders, mentors and ecosystem experts for two days of learning, collaboration and industry engagement. 

The sessions focused on: 
- Go-to-Market Strategies to strengthen market adoption 
- Startup Storytelling & Pitching to communicate solutions effectively 
- Investment Readiness and creating value with corporate investors 
- Building for Bharat through practical entrepreneurial insights 

A key highlight was the panel discussion, "From Proof of Concept to Scale: Making Corporate-Startup Partnerships Work," which brought together leaders from Pernod Ricard India, Shell, MiniMines and Prakrithi Ventures to explore how startups and corporates can move beyond pilots towards meaningful partnerships and implementation. 

The bootcamp also marked an important milestone with the signing of an MoU by BeST - Bengaluru Science and Technology Cluster (initiative of the Office of PSA, GoI) and NSRCEL, alongside leadership interactions, founder networking and grant evaluation pitches. 

As the 12 startups begin their incubation journey, the focus remains on strengthening their solutions, accessing market opportunities and building connections across the circular economy ecosystem.

Thank you, Bryan Danielson. And thanks to Prof. William Barnett and Stanford University Graduate School of Business for deciding that Social Alpha's work belonged in a classroom.

I read Prof. Christopher Marquis essay with more sympathy than you might expect. He is right that too many cases celebrate winners and decision-makers. He is right that “win-win” has become a comfortable bedtime story.

Social Alpha exists because markets routinely fail the people who need them most. The smallholder woman farmer. The rural patient. The innovation no investor will underwrite because the risk is real and the return is social.

That's why this case matters, and why Bryan's clarity in writing it matters.

A non-profit that builds markets where markets fail, and measures success by how soon it becomes irrelevant, is not the usual protagonist of a business school case. No exit. No valuation. No unicorn. Just failures, dead ends and unfinished work, and a case that still keeps them in. 

When a leading business school decides that is worth teaching, it says something. Not that business schools have solved their problems, or that Prof. Marquis’s critique lacks merit. That they can still learn from those who work outside the usual script.

Capitalism will not be reimagined by abolishing the places where future managers are trained. It will be reimagined by putting different questions in front of them. Who carries the risk? Whom is the market failing? What would it take to make a solution so ordinary that nobody needs us any more? 

The engineers and doctors Prof. Marquis wants to protect deserve to wrestle with those questions. We would be glad to meet them.

Thank you again, Bryan, for starting this conversation

A working prototype. A deeply personal mission. And a regulatory journey they hadn't anticipated. 

When Anirban Palit and his wife, Dr. Sayantani Pramanik , Ph.D., began working on CERVICHECK, they did not just want to make better tests. They wanted to make cervical cancer screening more accessible. They had seen how the discomfort of pelvic exams could discourage women from screening. They had also lost someone close to them to cervical cancer that was detected too late. 

They built an at-home HPV self-sampling kit that worked beautifully in the lab. But as many medtech founders learn, this is only the beginning. 

Because their device was classified as a non-predicate Class B medical device, there was no existing playbook for regulatory approval. What they thought would be a 6-month process turned into a massive mountain of compliance, clinical protocols, and Quality Management Systems (QMS). 

That is where our regulatory experts at Venture Center stepped in. We didn't just hand them a stack of templates. Our teams worked alongside them almost daily to demystify QMS standards, connect them with the right CRO, and give them access to our ISO-certified MedTech Cleanroom so they could manufacture their pilot batches.

Every milestone has a story. As Venture Center celebrates 20 years, we’re sharing the stories behind the milestones that matter.
